Energy and Simple Machines
1.1 What is Energy?
Energy is the capacity of a body to do work. Energy is measured in joules. A body can store energy because of its motion or because of its position. The total energy of an isolated system stays constant; energy only changes from one form to another. This idea is called the law of conservation of energy.

Energy is the capacity of a body to do work. Energy is measured in joules. A body can store energy because of its motion or because of its position. The total energy of an isolated system stays constant; energy only changes from one form to another. This idea is called the law of conservation of energy.

pages.raw_text:
1.2 Kinetic Energy
The energy a body has because of its motion is called kinetic energy. A rolling ball, flowing water and a moving car all have kinetic energy. Kinetic energy equals one half of the mass multiplied by the square of the speed, written as KE = 1/2 m v^2. Doubling the speed of a car makes its kinetic energy four times larger, which is why fast cars need much longer distances to stop.

pages.raw_text:
1.3 Potential Energy
The energy stored in a body because of its position or shape is called potential energy. Water held behind a dam and a stretched rubber band both store potential energy. Gravitational potential energy equals mass times gravitational acceleration times height, written as PE = m g h. When the water is released it falls and its potential energy turns into kinetic energy that can spin a turbine.

2.1 Levers
A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum. The force applied to the lever is the effort and the weight being moved is the load. A seesaw, a pair of scissors and a crowbar are all levers. Placing the fulcrum close to the load lets a small effort lift a heavy load. Figure 2.1 Parts of a lever: effort, fulcrum and load.

2.2 Pulleys
A pulley is a wheel with a groove around its rim that carries a rope. A single fixed pulley does not reduce the effort, but it changes the direction of the force, so you can pull down to lift a load up. Combining several pulleys in a block and tackle reduces the effort needed, because the load is shared between several sections of rope. Cranes on building sites use block and tackle systems.

pages.raw_text:
2.3 Mechanical Advantage and Efficiency
Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the load to the effort. A machine with a mechanical advantage of four lets an effort of 100 newtons move a load of 400 newtons. Efficiency is the useful work output divided by the work input, usually given as a percentage. No real machine is 100 percent efficient because some energy is always lost as heat through friction. Oiling the moving parts reduces friction and raises efficiency.
